text: So the agent registry makes agents legible, and it registers, retrieves, and discovers the key facts about agents that we want to know for any agent. So those are things like which tools it declares, what endpoints it's going to talk to, which product does it belong to, who owns it. And humans, other programs, other agents can then use the agent registry to decide what's available at the firm, whether that's useful for them, and to go use that as a source of truth for other questions. So this doesn't require extra effort on your part. It just happens when you use one of the firm's approved agent building frameworks. It's automatically registered. All that information is recorded there for you. And if you want to do a manual registration, you can certainly do that. So the second problem we have is that now that we've got all these agents doing all these things, we quickly notice that what they're doing is really different. And that means our agents carry really different risks, right? So a thing that summarizes JIRA or linear tickets is really different than a production deployment agent that can touch a running system. And if we try to use the same review process to cover all of these agents, then every agent is waiting in the same queue for weeks for human review. And if people are going to route around slow processes, then we wind up in the same situation that we had before. So, again, you might be tempted to say the answer is something like really detailed, heavy manual review by all of these different constituencies. Again, that feels safe, but now we've got a trivial summarizer waiting two months for the same sign-offs as an agent that is touching production systems. And most of the good agent ideas, most of the ones that have value right away, start out as small experiments, and you don't want those people to wait in the same line as the stuff that's touching production right away. So the reviewers are drowning in these, like, low-risk requests, and the high-risk ones have to share that attention pool. So we don't want to trade away that speed if we can help it. So again, because not every agent needs the same review, and because most agents are purpose-built rather than open-ended, when I say open-ended here, you can imagine coding agents like Py or Cloud Code. When you open them and you start typing, Cloud Code or Py doesn't know what you're about to ask. It doesn't circumscribe its purpose in any particular way. But most of the agents that are deployed in enterprises do have very specific purposes. When you're engaging with that agent, it's to do something specific that's well-known and well-understood. So they have a very specific reason for existing and a very circumscribed purpose. And you can tell these agents apart from each other by looking at what they declare up front, their tools, the endpoints they access, the controls that are applied to them, et cetera. So the third problem is that if you know about your agents and what they're doing, you'll quickly notice that many agents don't talk to just one thing or in just one capacity. The more open-ended the agent is, the more it looks like a Cloud Code or Py, the more it can do a variety and a diversity of different things, call an internal API, run a tool like a web search, that sort of thing. And each one of those is opening a different door to a different kind of risk. And if you give an agent an entitlement for a role account, then it can do a lot more damage than something that's just going to read a public web page, for example. So the question is not, can this agent do X, but what's the granularity that we need to solve for for the agent to act successfully? And again, one tempting answer is to kind of be heavy-handed here or to give every agent the same short allow list of stuff that's safe to do and then block everything else. That's safe, but it's also useless. An agent that can't search or can't call an API or can't do any of those things without asking somebody first can't really do the work that it was intended for. And then teams either give up on those agents or they find a way around the wall, and both outcomes are costly. So a wide kind of blanket block on everything trades away the innovation that we want to preserve and avoids making a real decision about risk. And as author John Shedd wrote, a ship and harbor is safe, but that is not what ships are for. So the fix here is to let agents declare their purpose up front and say what tools they're going to use or what tools they need access to. So in the second column here, we might say that a research summarizer is going to be allowed to use a web tool to access research, but for a release deployer agent, we're not going to allow them to do that because they have no reason to use that tool. And so if they try to ask for it, they won't get it by default. So we don't need to make this kind of decision for every tool. The agents just have to say which tools they want. And you're, as the agent author, you're in the best position to say, I need these four things out of the 500 that are available. So the way we need to enforce that is that when agents run in our managed environments, they look at the registry that we talked about before to look up what policies apply to it at initialization time. And that policy gets translated into enforceable statements like which endpoints are you allowed to access, which hosts are you allowed to access, what other types of resources are available or not available to you. And in this way, nobody's writing a ticket every time they need to change the access. Nobody's going to talk to IT or some other group outside of your team. As long as you conform to the risk score that we talked about before and you're in the agent registry, you're governed, you're approved. So this is how we keep the cost to teams really low for deploying, building, running agents. And this same control architecture works in a variety of settings. The next thing we noticed was that teams were building a ton of different ways to evaluate agents and every stack looks different. And some teams don't build anything at all. Sometimes you build this really detailed stack for how your models work. Sometimes there's nothing. And I think in general, we'd be upset if teams were not writing unit tests. We consider evals to be kind of the same thing. If models are changing, that's like a runtime dependency that your application has. And if your agent is going to change models, it doesn't know without the evals what's going to happen to its outputs and to the quality of those outputs. So again, one tempting answer here is let's have some kind of central evaluation methodology that waits for a full eval suite and a committee sign off. But now every prompt tweak, every one-line change is going to sit in that same queue. So we don't want to put more decisions on more reviewers for things like that. We don't want to trade away that iteration. So again, you wouldn't ship software without unit tests. So agents need evaluations for the same reason. And we want to provide the stuff at the level of the firm that's going to be the same for everybody. So team A writing evals, team B writing evals. They're both going to have many of the same features. So we want to have one shared approach to how we do evals and have the shared approach be something that's run by the firm and available to everybody for doing their evals. So that covers all the common parts of evals, and all you've got to do is just write what's true about your agent. And finally, maybe you've had the experience of being asked to approve lots and lots of individual agent actions when there's a human in the loop. So that's fine at a small scale, but once you're operating agents in parallel or in production, this becomes completely onerous, and review requests come in faster than anybody can be expected to approve them. After the first few times of this happening, you succumb to review fatigue, where you just see yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, and eventually you click yes on something that's activating the nuclear bomb. So you don't want to click yes by reflex, but that's going to happen inevitably. One recent example of this is earlier this year, a director at an AI research lab told her open-claw agent to suggest emails to delete from her inbox and wait for her approval, but her inbox was so large that eventually the agent compacted its context and lost the part that said, wait for my approval, and then it deleted hundreds of emails and didn't stop when she told it to stop on her phone. So again, you might be tempted to make a human approve every action, but that's not the right way to do it. A better approach is to let these independent, conservative classifiers make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference. If you're saying yes 99.99999% of the time, then that's probably just a rule that the agent should follow, not a request you need to ask the human for permission for. And the stuff that's unclear or ambiguous or potentially dangerous, yes, surface that to a human, or if it's definitely just dangerous, deny it outright. So this is a way to not have to do all the review work all the time. So we don't want to take the same approach for both explicit, when explicit rules apply, we want deterministic fast paths. When explicit rules don't apply and there's some ambiguity, we want a classifier to do that work instead. So putting those five pieces back together, you create a registry so every agent's visible from the day it's created. You score each agent so human review goes in the right spot. You run agents on guardrails so that they only touch what they need. You share evals and metrics so everybody's reaching the same bar without having to reinvent the wheel. And then finally you govern your run time to make sure that classification happens there and not somewhere else. So each of these controls works together. So I'll leave you with one question. Why do cars have brakes? It's not just so that you can stop, it's so that you can go fast and stop safely. So controls for our agents works the same way. Thank you very much. I'm John Feminello, and I hope you had a good time.
